narrative:
The model estimated a 43% probability that you would be a bad credit risk—roughly 43 in 100 applicants with a similar profile would be expected to have repayment difficulty. Under the lender’s decision rule, that estimated risk was high enough to deny the application.

The strongest influence on the decision was the length of the credit request. You asked for 48 months, far longer than the roughly 19 months typical among approved applicants, and this factor pushed the prediction most strongly toward bad credit. The second most important factor was your credit history; it leaned toward good credit in the model’s assessment, though past delays are uncommon among approved applicants, so it is worth checking for accuracy. The third was how long you have been employed; this also leaned toward good credit, even though your current status is unemployed. In short, the long requested repayment period was the dominant concern and outweighed the two moderating factors.

To improve your chances, ask the lender for the specific reasons recorded for the denial and focus on reducing the repayment period or requested amount. Providing evidence of stable income or a suitable guarantor, correcting any credit-report errors, and reapplying when your employment and credit record are stronger would also help.
